s.d: to lose one’s motivation to accomplish some valid goal
s.g: to become discouraged; to lose heart; to give up
s.c: In place of a negative expression such as ‘not to give up,’ it may be better in some languages to use a positive equivalent, for example, ‘to keep on’ or ‘to continue.’

s.d: pertaining to there being no cause or legitimate reason
s.g: without cause; without reason; for no reason

s.d: pertaining to being without any result
s.g: in vain; to no avail; with no result
s.c: In a number of languages an expression such as ‘to be without results’ may be rendered as ‘will accomplish nothing’ or ‘will be as though it had never happened.’

s.d: pertaining to being without purpose
s.g: for no purpose; without purpose

s.d: cardinal number, where there are twenty instances of a countable entity
s.g: twenty

s.d: to give in to a superior power or force
s.g: to give in to; to surrender; to yield

s.d: an object (not necessarily three-dimensional) which has been formed to resemble a person, god, animal, etc.
s.g: likeness; image
s.c: In certain contexts the referents of εἰκών, τύπος, and χάραγμα may have special religious significance in that they may refer to idols, but the focal component for the translator is that of a likeness or resemblance (see LN 58.35). In contexts such as ⟦Matthew 22:20|Matthew 22:20⟧ an equivalent translation may be simply ‘a picture,’ but in ⟦Romans 1:23|Romans 1:23⟧ and ⟦Acts 7:43|Acts 7:43⟧ one may use the same expression as is employed to render εἴδωλον ‘idol’ (LN 6.97).

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Same or Equivalent Kind or Class
s.d: that which has the same form as something else
s.g: same form; likeness
s.c: Since the expressions τοῦ χοϊκοῦ and τοῦ ἐπουρανίου refer to individuals, it is much more satisfactory to translate ⟦1 Corinthians 15:49|1 Corinthians 15:49⟧ as ‘just as we have the likeness of the man made of earth, so we will have the likeness of the Man from heaven.’|In ⟦1 Corinthians 15:49|1 Corinthians 15:49⟧ εἰκών designates similarity in class or kind, while in ⟦Romans 1:23|Romans 1:23⟧ εἰκών indicates a fashioned object (see LN 6.96).

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
s.d: that which represents something else in terms of basic form and features
s.g: representation; pattern

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Honesty, Sincerity
s.d: the quality of sincerity as an expression of pure or unadulterated motives
s.g: sincerity; purity of motives

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Honesty, Sincerity
s.d: pertaining to being sincere in the sense of having pure motivation
s.g: sincere; without hidden motives

s.d: an emphatic marker of condition
s.g: if indeed; if after all

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Peaceful Behavior
s.d: to live in peace with others
s.g: to behave peacefully; to live in peace
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘live in peace’ is a negation of fighting, for example, ‘do not fight’ or ‘do not constantly quarrel.’

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Favorable Circumstances or State
s.d: a set of favorable circumstances involving peace and tranquility
s.g: peace; tranquility
s.c: The meaning of ‘peace’ or ‘tranquility’ may be expressed in some languages in a negative form, for example, ‘to be without trouble’ or ‘to have no worries’ or ‘to sit down in one’s heart.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: a state of freedom from anxiety and inner turmoil{N:001}
s.g: peace; freedom from worry
s.c: ‘Peace’ in the sense of ‘freedom from worry’ is often expressed by means of an idiom, for example, ‘to sit down in the heart,’ ‘to rest in the liver,’ or ‘to be quiet in one’s inner self.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: pertaining to freedom from anxiety and inner turmoil
s.g: peaceful; free from worry

s.d: to cause a state of peace or reconciliation between persons
s.g: to make peace; to make things right
s.c: εἰρηνοποιέω is closely related in meaning to the series in LN 40.1 in that the making of peace or reestablishing peace between persons is a distinctive feature of reconciliation, but the focus in εἰρηνοποιέω seems to be upon the resulting state rather than upon the process.

s.d: (derivative of {L:εἰρηνοποιέω<SDBG:εἰρηνοποιέω:000000>} ‘to make peace,’ {D:40.4}) a person who restores peace between people
s.g: peacemaker; one who works for peace
s.c: Though in ⟦Matthew 5:9|Matthew 5:9⟧ the cessation of war is by no means excluded, the focus of meaning of εἰρηνοποιός is reconciliation between persons and not primarily to cause wars to cease.

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension To a Goal
s.d: extension toward a special goal{N:001}
s.g: to; toward; in the direction of

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension To a Goal
s.d: extension toward a goal which is inside an area
s.g: into

s.dp: Spacial Positions › On, Upon, On the Surface Of
s.d: a position on the surface of an area
s.g: on; at

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Among, Between, In, Inside
s.d: a position defined as being within certain limits{N:002}
s.g: inside; within; in

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Among, Between, In, Inside
s.d: a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects{N:003}
s.g: among; with

s.d: a marker of intent, often with the implication of expected result
s.g: for the purpose of; in order to

s.d: a marker of result, with the probable implication of a preceding process
s.g: with the result that; so that as a result; to cause
s.c: It is also possible to interpret εἰς in this construction of ⟦2 Thessalonians 1:5|2 Thessalonians 1:5⟧ as purpose (see εἰς, LN 89.57).|It would be possible to interpret εἰς … ἄγω in ⟦Romans 2:4|Romans 2:4⟧ as being purely an expression of cause since ἄγω (see LN 36.1) also involves a component of cause, and therefore one may interpret the expression εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει as ‘it causes you to repent.’ In either case, however, εἰς marks a resulting event or state.

s.d: a marker of the means by which one event makes another event possible{N:004}
s.g: by means of; through; by

s.d: (with the accusative) a marker of content as a means of specifying a particular referent
s.g: concerning; with respect to; with reference to; about; in

s.dp: Degree › Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
s.d: a degree extending to a particular point as marked by the context
s.g: to the point of; to the extent of; to the degree that; up to
s.c: In ⟦2 Corinthians 10:15|2 Corinthians 10:15⟧ περισσείαν itself indicates a superabundant degree of something (see LN 78.31), while εἰς marks a degree up to such a point. One may say, therefore, that semantically εἰς serves to reinforce the meaning of περισσείαν.

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: a marker of a change of state
s.g: from … to; to; for

s.d: a marker of an involved experiencer
s.g: to; toward; for
s.c: It is possible to translate ⟦1 Peter 1:11|1 Peter 1:11⟧ as ‘trying to find out when the time would be and how it would come’ by interpreting εἰς in ⟦1 Peter 1:11|1 Peter 1:11⟧ as εἰς (LN 90.23) and ποῖον as ποῖος (LN 58.30).

s.d: (with the accusative) a marker of persons benefited by an event, with the implication of something directed to them
s.g: for; on behalf of
s.c: In both ⟦1 Corinthians 16:1|1 Corinthians 16:1⟧ and ⟦2 Corinthians 8:4|2 Corinthians 8:4⟧ there is clearly an ellipsis of an event of ‘sending’ such help to and on behalf of God’s people.

s.d: (with the dative) a marker of objects which serve as symbolic substitutes for supernatural persons or powers presumed to act as guarantors of compliance with oaths
s.g: by

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: a marker of an extent of time
s.g: for; in; at
s.c: For another interpretation of εἰς τέλος in ⟦1 Thessalonians 2:16|1 Thessalonians 2:16⟧ (as an idiom), see LN 78.47.

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: a marker of a unit of time
s.g: on; at; for

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: the continuous extent of time up to a point
s.g: until; to; at last; at length
s.c: The phrase εἰ μὴ ὅταν is often translated as ‘until’ (for example, μηδενὶ ἅ εἶδον διηγήσωνται, εἰ μὴ ὅταν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ ‘not to tell anybody what they have seen until the Son of Man has risen from death’ ⟦Mark 9:9|Mark 9:9⟧), but this phrase may be analyzed as meaning ‘if it is not when,’ an expression which is semantically equivalent to ‘until.’|For an interpretation of εἰς τέλος in ⟦John 13:1|John 13:1⟧ as an idiom, see LN 78.47.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to come into knowledge) to acquire information about something, with emphasis upon the process involved
s.g: to learn about; to find out; to come to know
s.c: It is also possible to treat the phrase εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἔρχομαι as meaning ‘to come to know’ in the sense of ‘to come to understand’ (see LN 32.17).

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to come into knowledge) to come to understand the meaning of something, with special emphasis upon the process
s.g: to come to understand; to come to know
s.c: One may also interpret εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἔρχομαι as meaning ‘to come to have knowledge of, to come to know’ (see LN 27.4).

s.d: (an idiom, literally: into that which is not measured) a point on a scale going beyond what is expected
s.g: excessive; beyond measure
s.c: In a number of languages one can perhaps best render this statement in ⟦2 Corinthians 10:13|2 Corinthians 10:13⟧ as ‘we will not boast too much’ or ‘we will boast only so much.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: unlimited duration of time, with particular focus upon the future
s.g: always; forever; forever and ever; eternally
s.c: See also ⟦Luke 1:33|Luke 1:33⟧; ⟦2 Peter 3:18|2 Peter 3:18⟧; ⟦Jude 1:25|Jude 1:25⟧; ⟦Hebrews 1:8|Hebrews 1:8⟧. The more elaborate expressions employing αἰών are somewhat more emphatic in meaning and are to be found especially in the solemn style of doxologies.|For another interpretation of εἰς τὸ παντελές in ⟦Hebrews 7:25|Hebrews 7:25⟧, see LN 78.47.

s.dp: Know › Not Able To Be Known, Secret
s.d: (an idiom, literally: into the ear) pertaining to what is known only by those who hear a particular message in private
s.g: in secret; in private; privately
s.c: A phrase such as ‘whatever you hear in secret’ may be rendered as ‘whatever you hear when no one else is listening.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to come to the worse) to become increasingly more sick
s.g: to get worse; to become more sick

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Envy, Jealousy
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in the gall of bitterness) to be particularly envious or resentful of someone
s.g: to be very jealous; to be terribly envious; to be bitterly envious

s.d: one, in contrast to more than one; cardinal number, where there is one instance of a countable entity
s.g: one

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Whom or What Spoken or Written About
s.d: a reference to a single, indefinite person or thing (sometimes reinforced by the indefinite reference τις[a], {D:92.12})
s.g: a; one

s.d: that which is united as one in contrast with being divided or consisting of separate parts
s.g: one
s.c: This phrase in ⟦Galatians 3:20|Galatians 3:20⟧ is a reference to the fact that God in the Scriptures is defined as a unit and not as being characterized by numerous manifestations or realizations.

s.d: to bring or lead into
s.g: to lead into; to take into

s.d: to carry or bring something into an area or structure
s.g: to bring in; to carry in

s.d: to listen to someone, with the implication of heeding and responding to what is heard
s.g: to listen to; to heed; to pay attention to what is said

s.d: to obey on the basis of having paid attention to{N:001}
s.g: to obey; obedience
s.c: Terms expressing the concept of ‘obedience’ may frequently be rendered in some languages as ‘to do what one says’ or ‘to carry out someone’s orders.’

s.d: to accept the presence of a person with friendliness{N:001}
s.g: to welcome; to receive; to accept; to have as a guest
s.c: In view of the fact that εἰσδέχομαι in ⟦2 Corinthians 6:17|2 Corinthians 6:17⟧ refers to God’s receiving people, it may be necessary to use quite a different expression than one would normally employ in referring to welcoming a guest into the home. In some instances one may use a rather generic expression such as ‘to accept,’ and this may be expressed idiomatically in some languages as ‘to extend my hand to you’ or ‘to count you as belonging to me.’ It is the figurative usage of εἰσδέχομαι in this type of context which may lead to a somewhat different type of rendering.

s.d: to move into a space, either two-dimensional or three-dimensional
s.g: to move into; to come into; to go into; to enter

s.d: to move into a space, either two-dimensional or three-dimensional
s.g: to move into; to come into; to go into; to enter
s.c: εἰσέρχομαι is also used in the NT in speaking of the entrance of demons or Satan into animate beings, for example, λέγοντες, Πέμψον ἡμᾶς εἰς τοὺς χοίρους, ἵνα εἰς αὐτοὺς εἰσέλθωμεν saying, Send us into the swine so we may enter them ⟦Mark 5:12|Mark 5:12⟧. In a number of languages one cannot speak of such supernatural beings ‘entering’ an object. It may be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to grab’ or ‘to control’ or ‘to command.’

s.d: to happen, with the focus upon the initial aspect
s.g: to happen; to come into
s.c: In some languages it may be impossible to speak of ‘sin coming’ (⟦Romans 5:12|Romans 5:12⟧), and therefore one may have to restructure the relationships, for example, ‘people began to sin.’

s.d: to begin, with the focus upon the initial stages of an activity
s.g: to begin; to commence
s.c: In the first clause of ⟦Luke 9:46|Luke 9:46⟧, it is clear that the event is to be found in the noun διαλογισμός, while the verb εἰσῆλθεν merely contributes an aspect of the event.

s.d: to begin to experience an event or state
s.g: to begin to experience; to come into an experience; to attain

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: (idiom, literally: to go in and to go out) to live or to conduct oneself in relationship to some community or group
s.g: to live with; to live among
s.c: The semantic focus of this idiom in ⟦Acts 1:21|Acts 1:21⟧ appears to be the manner in which a person conducts himself in relationship to others, but it is possible to imply a certain amount of movement. For example, in ⟦Acts 1:21|Acts 1:21⟧, it is possible to translate ‘during the whole time the Lord Jesus travelled about with us.’

s.d: to invite a person in as a guest
s.g: to invite in

s.dp: Linear Movement › Come, Come To, Arrive
s.d: to come to or to arrive at the scene of action
s.g: coming; arrival

s.d: welcome extended to a person on the occasion of a visit, with probable focus upon the ready acceptance
s.g: welcome; acceptance

s.d: to run or rush quickly in to
s.g: to run into; to rush into

s.d: to run or rush out quickly
s.g: to run out; to rush out

s.d: to move into a space, either two-dimensional or three-dimensional
s.g: to move into; to come into; to go into; to enter

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: (idiom, literally: to go in and to go out) to live or to conduct oneself in relationship to some community or group
s.g: to live with; to live among
s.c: The semantic focus of this idiom in ⟦Acts 9:28|Acts 9:28⟧ appears to be the manner in which a person conducts himself in relationship to others, but it is possible to imply a certain amount of movement. For example, in ⟦Acts 9:28|Acts 9:28⟧ one could translate ‘Paul stayed with them and went about in Jerusalem.’

s.g: to run in; to run into

s.d: to carry or bring something into an area or structure
s.g: to bring in; to carry in

s.d: to cause someone to enter into a particular event or state
s.g: to cause to; to bring in to; to lead to

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to bring into the ears) to cause someone to hear
s.g: to cause to hear; to make hear
s.c: In a number of languages, however, it is awkward to speak of ‘to cause to hear’; rather, it seems far better to use an expression of ‘speaking,’ for example, ‘what we hear you say is strange.’ For another interpretation of this idiom in ⟦Acts 17:20|Acts 17:20⟧, see LN 33.92.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to bring into the ears) to bring something to the attention of people by means of speech, but probably not in a formal or open manner
s.g: to bring to the attention of; to speak about to
s.c: For another interpretation of this idiom in ⟦Acts 17:20|Acts 17:20⟧, see LN 24.55.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time following another point{N:001}
s.g: then; afterwards; later

s.d: a marker of an addition which has just been specified in the context
s.g: besides this; furthermore

s.d: (normally a doublet, but in {S:04601402700002} occurring singly) a double or multiple marker of condition (equivalent in meaning to {L:εἰ<SDBG:εἰ:000000>}[a] ‘if,’ {D:89.65})
s.g: if … if; whether … or

s.dp: Spacial Extensions › Extension From a Source
s.d: extension from an area or space, usually with the implication of removal out of a delimited area
s.g: from; out from; out of

s.d: a marker of cause or reason, with focus upon the source{N:002}
s.g: because of

s.d: a marker of means as constituting a source
s.g: by means of; from
s.c: Some scholars have interpreted ἐκ in ⟦Luke 16:9|Luke 16:9⟧ as ἐκ ‘apart from’ (see LN 89.121). This requires the reading of ἐκλίπητε (found in a few late manuscripts) for ἐκλίπω in ⟦Luke 16:9|Luke 16:9⟧b.

s.d: (with the genitive) a marker of instrument, with the added implication of result
s.g: by; as a result of

s.d: a marker of manner, often with the implication of source
s.g: with; from

s.dp: Case › Source of Event or Activity
s.d: (with the genitive) a marker of the source of an activity or state, with the implication of something proceeding from or out of the source
s.g: from; by

s.d: a marker of dissociation in the sense of being independent from someone or something
s.g: from; free from; apart from; independent of
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 9:19|1 Corinthians 9:19⟧ it may be valuable to relate the first part of the verse to what immediately follows, for example, ‘for I am not a slave of anyone, but I make myself a slave to everyone’ or ‘though I am not anyone’s slave, I serve everyone.’

s.d: a marker of the source from which someone or something is physically or psychologically derived
s.g: from

s.d: a marker of a part of a whole, whether consisting of countables or of mass
s.g: one of; one among; a part of

s.d: a marker of the aspect of cessation
s.g: from

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a marker of a point of time which is simultaneous to or overlaps with another point of time{N:003}
s.g: when; at the time of

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: a marker of the extent of time from a point in the past
s.g: since; from

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Pay, Price, Cost
s.d: a marker of price
s.g: with; by means of

s.d: a marker of the substance of which something consists or out of which it is made
s.g: of; consisting of; out of; made of

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to sit on the right side of) to be in a position of high status
s.g: to sit on the right side of; to be granted high position
s.c: Compare the use of ἀριστερός in LN 87.35 and see the discussion of ⟦Mark 10:37|Mark 10:37⟧ there. For another interpretation of δεξιός in ⟦Mark 10:37|Mark 10:37⟧, see LN 82.8.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: from a part) the state of being part of something
s.g: being part of; as a part of; in part; partially

s.d: (an idiom, literally: from measure) a scalar point marking considerable limitation in the extent of some activity
s.g: sparingly; in a limited way
s.c: In a number of languages this expression in ⟦John 3:34|John 3:34⟧ may be appropriately rendered as ‘he doesn’t hold back at all when he gives the Spirit’ or ‘he gives the Spirit in an abundant way.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: from excess) an extremely high point on a scale of extent and implying excess
s.g: exceedingly; extremely; decidedly; excessively
s.c: In ⟦Mark 6:51|Mark 6:51⟧ both λίαν (LN 78.1) and ἐκ περισσοῦ are expressions of degree and they reinforce one another.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: an exceedingly long period of time from an assumed beginning up to the present
s.g: since all time; from all ages past; from the beginning of time

s.d: (an idiomatic frame, literally: from … to …) a degree of totality emphasizing exclusiveness or the elimination of other possibilities
s.g: completely; entirely; exclusively a matter of

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to sit on the left side of) to be in a position of high status, but less than in the case of the right side (compare {D:87.34})
s.g: to be given somewhat less high status; to sit on the left side of
s.c: Compare the use of δεξιός in LN 87.34.|In a number of languages the equivalent of this entire expression in ⟦Mark 10:37|Mark 10:37⟧ would be ‘in order that one of us may be number one and the other may be number two in your kingdom’ or ‘in order that one of us may be your first officer and the other your second officer in your kingdom.’ For another interpretation of ἀριστερός in ⟦Mark 10:37|Mark 10:37⟧, see LN 82.7.

s.dp: Spacial Positions › Opposite, Over Against, Across From, Offshore From
s.d: a position over against an object or other position
s.g: opposite; in front of; before; across from; in the presence of

s.d: pertaining to being hostile toward
s.g: hostile; one who is hostile

s.d: each one of a totality in a distributive sense
s.g: each

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: duration of time, with reference to a series of occasions
s.g: always; at all times; on every occasion

s.d: cardinal number, where there are one hundred instances of a countable entity
s.g: one hundred

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: pertaining to a period of a hundred years
s.g: hundred years

s.dp: Number › Double, Four Times As Much, Etc. [Multiples]
s.d: one hundred times as much in quantity
s.g: a hundred times; a hundred times as much

s.d: a Roman officer in command of about one hundred men
s.g: centurion; captain
s.c: In a number of languages, centurion can very readily be rendered by a phrase such as ‘a commander of a hundred soldiers,’ but in many instances the closest natural equivalent is simply ‘captain.’

s.d: to throw out of an area or object
s.g: to throw out; to jettison (from a boat)
s.c: It may be that ἐκβάλλω in ⟦Matthew 21:39|Matthew 21:39⟧ is a type of hyperbole for causing to go out, but at the same time it is possible that the term ἐκβάλλω is to be understood in a literal sense.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to cause to go out or leave, often, but not always, involving force
s.g: to send away; to drive out; to expel
s.c: In referring to exorcism of evil spirits, it may be necessary in some languages to use figurative expressions, for example, ‘to pull out,’ ‘to cause to to dismount,’ or ‘to cause one’s heart to return.’

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to send out or away from, presumably for some purpose
s.g: to send; to send out; to send forth

s.d: to lead or bring out of a structure or area
s.g: to lead out; to bring forth

s.d: to cause a demon to no longer possess or control a person
s.g: to cast out; to make go out; to exorcise
s.c: The process of exorcism is expressed in different languages in a number of diverse ways, for example, ‘to make leave,’ ‘to chase away,’ ‘to force to run,’ ‘to destroy,’ ‘to overpower,’ or ‘to kill.’

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: to cause a significant change of state by decisive action
s.g: to cause to be; to make become
s.c: In some languages, however, it may be extremely difficult to speak of ‘justice prevailing.’ The closest equivalent may be ‘until he causes all people to be treated justly’ or ‘until authorities treat all people in a just manner.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to throw out the name) to insult or slander, with a possible implication of a kind of psychological ostracism
s.g: to insult; to slander

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἔκβασις ‘way out of,’ not occurring in the NT) the end point of a duration, but often with the implication of outcome or result
s.g: end
s.c: For another interpretation of ἔκβασις in ⟦Hebrews 13:7|Hebrews 13:7⟧, see LN 89.39.

s.d: the outcome of an event or state
s.g: result; outcome

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: a congregation of Christians, implying interacting membership
s.g: congregation; church
s.c: Though some persons have tried to see in the term ἐκκλησία a more or less literal meaning of ‘called-out ones,’ this type of etymologizing is not warranted either by the meaning of ἐκκλησία in NT times or even by its earlier usage. The term ἐκκλησία was in common usage for several hundred years before the Christian era and was used to refer to an assembly of persons constituted by well-defined membership. In general Greek usage it was normally a socio-political entity based upon citizenship in a city-state (see ἐκκλησία, LN 11.78) and in this sense is parallel to δῆμος (LN 11.78). For the NT, however, it is important to understand the meaning of ἐκκλησία as ‘an assembly of God’s people.’|In the rendering of ἐκκλησία a translator must beware of using a term which refers primarily to a building rather than to a congregation of believers. In many contexts ἐκκλησία may be readily rendered as ‘gathering of believers’ or ‘group of those who trust in Christ.’ Sometimes, as in ⟦1 Corinthians 1:2|1 Corinthians 1:2⟧, it is possible to translate ‘Paul writes to the believers in Christ who live in Corinth.’ Such a translation does, however, omit a significant element in the term ἐκκλησία, in that the sense of corporate unity is not specified.

But in the NT one cannot distinguish clearly between the meanings of these two words.|ἐκκλησία and δῆμος may be rendered in some languages as ‘a meeting of the people who belonged to that place’ or ‘… who were inhabitants of that town’ or ‘… whose homes were in that town.’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: pertaining to a point of time preceding another point of time, with an interval of considerable length{N:001}
s.g: long ago; of long ago
s.c: References to a point of time preceding another point of time may express a relationship to an event in the discourse or to the time of the discourse itself. In ⟦Hebrews 1:1|Hebrews 1:1⟧ πάλαι marks a point of time long before the actual writing of this Letter to the Hebrews. The same is true of ἔκπαλαι in ⟦2 Peter 3:5|2 Peter 3:5⟧. In some languages it is necessary to indicate clearly whether the interval is (1) between a prior time and the event mentioned in the discourse or (2) between a prior time and the discourse itself. For example, in ⟦Hebrews 1:1|Hebrews 1:1⟧ it may be necessary to translate ‘long ago before now God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets’ or ‘long ago before now that I am writing …’
